```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
library(patchwork)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What this notebook is

The mutant group had a genuinely good idea: instead of looking at a volcano plot,
**plot the fold change of every protein against where its gene sits on the
chromosome**. They did that for `stp_vs_anc_at_TSB` and `stk_vs_anc_at_TSB` and found
two regions per contrast where many neighbouring proteins move together. This notebook
(1) reproduces that, (2) puts a number on "clearly above noise" with a permutation test,
(3) asks what the regions actually are — and the answer is **not** signalling,
(4) repeats the whole scan on the two **interaction** contrasts, and
(5) takes all of it into the **phospho** data.

**The short version:** the two biggest "peaks" are almost certainly *genomic* differences
between the strains, not Stk1/Stp1-dependent regulation — and the phospho samples, an
independent preparation, confirm one of them. The interaction contrasts remove both by
construction, and what survives is a **secreted / cell-surface** signature. Along the way
the phospho data hands us the cleanest signalling result in the whole data set:
**ReoM Thr7 phosphorylation is completely absent from the `stk` mutant and completely
intact in `stp`** — see §6.4.
:::

## 1. Setup: the data plus a genomic axis

The DEA tables are keyed by `protein_key`; the coordinates live in the protein metadata
table that ships with the repository. One join gives every fold change a position on the
JE2 chromosome (CP020619.1, 2.87 Mb).

```{r data}
meta <- read_protein_metadata(cds_only = TRUE) |>
  select(protein_key, locus_tag, gene = gene_symbol_best, start, end, strand,
         product, up_protein_name, uniprot_acc, ortholog_quality)

dea <- read_dea("total") |>
  inner_join(select(meta, protein_key, gene, start, end, strand, up_protein_name),
             by = "protein_key") |>
  arrange(start)

# The six contrasts this notebook uses.
CONTRASTS_MAIN <- c("stp_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stk_vs_anc_at_TSB")
CONTRASTS_INT  <- c("interaction_stp_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN",
                    "interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN")

cat(sapply(c(CONTRASTS_MAIN, CONTRASTS_INT), explain_contrast), sep = "\n\n")
```

So for the **main** contrasts, `diff > 0` means **higher in the mutant** than in the
wild type. For the **interaction** contrasts, `diff > 0` means the mutant-minus-wild-type
difference is **larger in TSB than in SN** — i.e. the mutant and the wild type respond
*differently* to long-term PASN.

```{r coverage}
tibble(
  what = c("proteins in the DEA (contaminants dropped)",
           "of those, with a genome coordinate",
           "measured values that are imputed from the LOD"),
  n = c(n_distinct(read_dea("total")$protein_key),
        n_distinct(dea$protein_key),
        sum(dea$estimate_type == "lod_imputed"))
)
```

The ~70 proteins without a coordinate are contaminants and six-frame pseudogene
translations. They cannot be placed on the chromosome and are simply absent from every
plot below.

## 2. Part A — redoing the group's plot

One point per protein, x = start of its gene, y = `diff`. The red line is a rolling
median over 5 neighbouring genes, which is what makes a "peak" visible: single proteins
jump around, but a *run* of neighbours moving the same way does not.

```{r manhattan-main}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Fold change against genomic position for the two contrasts the group looked at. Red = rolling median over 5 neighbouring genes."

roll_median <- function(v, k = 5) zoo::rollapply(v, k, median, fill = NA, align = "center")

manhattan <- function(d, contrasts, k = 5, title = NULL) {
  x <- d |>
    filter(contrast %in% contrasts) |>
    group_by(contrast) |>
    arrange(start, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(roll = roll_median(diff, k)) |>
    ungroup()

  ggplot(x, aes(start / 1e6, diff)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.35) +
    geom_line(aes(y = roll), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~contrast, ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "position on the JE2 chromosome (Mb)",
         y = "diff (log2 fold change)", title = title)
}

manhattan(dea, CONTRASTS_MAIN)
```

Two things jump out, one per contrast:

* **`stk_vs_anc_at_TSB`**: a sharp spike just past 2.19 Mb, sitting on what looks like a
  broad raised plateau from roughly 2.18 to 2.29 Mb.
* **`stp_vs_anc_at_TSB`**: a deep, wide trough around 2.10–2.12 Mb.

That is exactly what the group described. Now let us put a number on it.

### 2.1 "Clearly above noise" — a permutation test

A rolling median looks convincing even in pure noise, so we need a null. The simplest
honest one: **keep the fold changes, shuffle which gene they belong to**. That destroys
genomic neighbourhood while keeping the distribution of `diff` exactly as it is. Anything
the real data does that 1000 shuffled genomes essentially never do is a real genomic
clustering.

The window size matters, and this turns out to be the whole point. A **narrow** window
(5 genes) is sensitive to a short, violent spike. A **wide** window (25 genes) is sensitive
to a long, modest plateau. We run both.

```{r permutation}
set.seed(42)

scan_genome <- function(d, contrast_name, k, n_perm = 1000) {
  x <- d |> filter(contrast == contrast_name) |> arrange(start)
  observed <- roll_median(x$diff, k)
  # Null: keep the fold changes, shuffle which gene they belong to.
  null_max <- replicate(n_perm, max(abs(roll_median(sample(x$diff), k)), na.rm = TRUE))
  x |> mutate(k = k,
              window_median = observed,
              threshold = quantile(null_max, 0.95),
              is_peak = !is.na(observed) & abs(observed) > threshold)
}

scans <- bind_rows(lapply(c(5, 25), \(k)
  bind_rows(lapply(c(CONTRASTS_MAIN, CONTRASTS_INT), \(cc) scan_genome(dea, cc, k)))))

scans |>
  group_by(k, contrast) |>
  summarise(threshold = round(first(threshold), 2),
            `windows above it` = sum(is_peak), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = k, values_from = c(threshold, `windows above it`))
```

```{r peak-regions}
# Merge neighbouring flagged windows into regions.
peak_regions <- scans |>
  group_by(k, contrast) |>
  mutate(idx = row_number()) |>
  filter(is_peak) |>
  mutate(region = cumsum(c(1, diff(idx) > k[1]))) |>
  group_by(k, contrast, region) |>
  summarise(from_Mb = round(min(start) / 1e6, 3),
            to_Mb   = round(max(start) / 1e6, 3),
            windows = n(),
            peak_window_median = round(window_median[which.max(abs(window_median))], 2),
            .groups = "drop")

peak_regions |> filter(windows >= 3) |> arrange(contrast, k)
```

Read that carefully, because it is more interesting than a simple "both peaks confirmed":

* The *stp* trough at **2.11–2.13 Mb** passes at **both** window sizes. It is a genuine,
  sharp, strong feature.
* The *stk* feature passes **only at the wide window**, as one long region from
  **2.17 to 2.28 Mb** — and it fails the narrow-window test completely (0 windows).

The wide scan also flags a few smaller regions the group did not mention — notably
0.88 Mb in `stp_vs_anc_at_TSB` (the *clfA*/*emp*/SaPI neighbourhood) and 2.10–2.12 Mb in
`interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN` (the φSa3 residue we come back to in §4.1). They are
weaker and we do not chase them here, but they are on the table.

That the *stk* feature fails the narrow test is not a weakness of the finding, it is a
**description** of it: the *stk*
feature is not a spike at all, it is a **broad plateau** of many genes each moved by a
modest, very similar amount. A test tuned to spikes cannot see it. The group drew the right
conclusion from the picture; the statistics just tell us the two features are of different
*kinds*. That difference turns out to be the key to what they are.

## 3. Part B — what are these two regions?

This is where the story turns. Both regions have an explanation that has nothing to do
with Ser/Thr signalling.

### 3.1 The *stk* region: a 107 kb block, and it is not a peak but a plateau

Zoom in. Note the two **rRNA operons** that flank the raised region almost exactly.

```{r rrn}
rrn <- read_tsv(file.path(REPO_ROOT, "data", "raw", "resources", "JE2_genome.gff"),
                comment = "#", col_names = c("seqid", "src", "type", "start", "end",
                                             "score", "strand", "phase", "attr"),
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(type == "rRNA", str_detect(attr, "16S|23S")) |>
  mutate(operon = cumsum(c(1, diff(start) > 10000))) |>
  group_by(operon) |>
  summarise(start = min(start), end = max(end), .groups = "drop")

rrn |> filter(start > 2.1e6, start < 2.4e6) |> mutate(across(c(start, end), ~ .x / 1e6))
```

```{r stk-block}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "stk_vs_anc_at_TSB around the raised region. Vertical grey bands: rRNA operons. Nearly every gene between them is up by about the same amount."

BLOCK <- c(2183000, 2291000)   # the two rrn operons bracket this

dea |>
  filter(contrast == "stk_vs_anc_at_TSB", start > 2.12e6, start < 2.36e6) |>
  ggplot(aes(start / 1e6, diff)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = rrn$start / 1e6, xmax = rrn$end / 1e6,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 0.7), linetype = c(1, 2), colour = c("grey60", "#D55E00")) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = start > BLOCK[1] & start < BLOCK[2]), size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2.12, 2.36)) +
  labs(x = "position (Mb)", y = "log2 FC, stk vs anc in TSB",
       caption = "dashed line: +0.7 = 1.6-fold")
```

```{r block-stats}
dea |>
  filter(contrast == "stk_vs_anc_at_TSB") |>
  mutate(region = if_else(start > BLOCK[1] & start < BLOCK[2], "inside block", "rest of genome")) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(proteins = n(),
            `median log2 FC` = round(median(diff), 2),
            `fold change` = round(2^median(diff), 2),
            `% above +0.3` = round(100 * mean(diff > 0.3)),
            .groups = "drop")
```

85 % of the 94 measured proteins in the block go up, against 13 % everywhere else, and the
whole block moves by the **same** amount (~1.65×). The edges are sharp to the single gene
and they coincide with the two rRNA operons.

**A coordinated 1.6-fold shift of every protein in one contiguous 107 kb segment, bounded
by two rRNA operons, is the classic signature of a tandem genomic amplification** —
recombination between two *rrn* copies duplicating everything in between. A regulatory
effect does not respect operon-independent genomic boundaries like that; gene dosage does.
1.6× rather than a clean 2× fits a duplication carried by part of the population.

Now the decisive check — rule 4 of `CLAUDE.md`. If this is a property of the *strain*, it
must be in **every** `stk` sample and in **every medium**, not just the TSB comparison:

```{r block-per-sample}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Median abundance of the 94 block proteins minus the median of the rest of the genome, per sample. Each point is one of the 27 samples."

ab <- read_abundances("total") |>
  inner_join(select(meta, protein_key, start), by = "protein_key")

block_shift <- ab |>
  mutate(region = case_when(start > BLOCK[1] & start < BLOCK[2] ~ "block",
                            start < 2177000 | start > 2299000   ~ "rest",
                            TRUE ~ NA_character_)) |>
  filter(!is.na(region)) |>
  group_by(sample, genotype, medium, region) |>
  summarise(md = median(normalized_abundance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = region, values_from = md) |>
  mutate(shift = block - rest)

ggplot(block_shift, aes(medium, shift, colour = genotype)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GENOTYPE_COLOURS) +
  labs(y = "block minus rest (log2)", x = NULL,
       title = "The block is up in all 9 stk samples, in all three media")
```

All nine `stk` samples sit about 0.6 log2 above all nine `anc` and all nine `stp` samples,
in every medium, with no overlap. This is a **constitutive property of the stk strain**.

What is inside the block matters, because it means the `stk` strain carries an extra copy
of these genes:

```{r block-content}
block_genes <- meta |> filter(start > BLOCK[1], start < BLOCK[2])

block_genes |>
  filter(!is.na(gene)) |>
  transmute(locus_tag, gene, start_Mb = round(start / 1e6, 3),
            protein = substr(coalesce(up_protein_name, product), 1, 55)) |>
  filter(gene %in% c("rsbW", "rsbV", "kdpA", "kdpB", "kdpC", "kdpD", "kdpE", "sceD",
                     "atpA", "atpB", "atpD", "atpG", "atpH", "murA", "glmS", "glmM",
                     "luxS", "ddl", "murF", "glyA", "dacA"))
```

Two of those are worth saying out loud:

* **`B7H15_11470` (the "RNA polymerase sigma factor" right next to `rsbW`/`rsbV`) is
  `sigB`** — the general stress sigma factor. The block contains the complete
  *rsbU-rsbV-rsbW-sigB* operon.
* The block also contains the **whole F1F0 ATP synthase operon** (`atpA/B/D/G/H`) and the
  **`kdp` potassium operon**.

```{r sigb-check}
meta |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_11465", "B7H15_11470", "B7H15_11475",
                          "B7H15_11480", "B7H15_11485")) |>
  transmute(locus_tag, gene, uniprot_acc,
            protein = substr(up_protein_name, 1, 60))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Consequence for the whole `stk` story
If the `stk` strain carries a duplication spanning *sigB*, then **any** σ^B^-dependent
difference between `stk` and `anc` has a second possible cause that has nothing to do with
the kinase. σ^B^ controls a large regulon in *S. aureus* including pigment, biofilm and
many of the very stress responses this course is about. This does not invalidate the
`stk` comparisons — but it means "Stk1 controls X" needs a stronger argument than "X is
different in the `stk` mutant".
:::

**Caveat, stated plainly:** proteomics cannot prove a DNA amplification. What we have shown
is a sharp, medium-independent, strain-specific, uniform 1.65-fold block bounded by *rrn*
operons. Amplification is the best explanation, but **whole-genome sequencing of the three
strains is what would settle it**, and it is cheap.

There is, however, a second measurement we can lean on: the **phospho-enriched** samples
are a separate preparation with their own normalisation, so they are a genuinely
independent look at the same strains. They confirm the block — see §6.1.

### 3.2 The *stp* region: the φSa3 prophage

```{r stp-prophage}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "stp_vs_anc_at_TSB across the prophage. The two hlb fragments (grey) mark where the phage is inserted into the beta-haemolysin gene."

hlb <- meta |> filter(gene == "hlb" | locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_10820", "B7H15_11175"))

dea |>
  filter(contrast == "stp_vs_anc_at_TSB", start > 2.075e6, start < 2.145e6) |>
  ggplot(aes(start / 1e6, diff)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = hlb$start / 1e6, xmax = hlb$end / 1e6 + 0.0008,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey75") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = estimate_type), size = 1.8, colour = "#009E73") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(observed = 16, lod_imputed = 1)) +
  labs(x = "position (Mb)", y = "log2 FC, stp vs anc in TSB",
       shape = NULL, caption = "open circles: at least one group mean imputed from the LOD")
```

The *hlb* gene (β-haemolysin) appears **twice** in the annotation, at 2.086 Mb and at
2.129 Mb. That is not an annotation error — it is a gene split in two by a prophage
inserted into it. In USA300/JE2 that is **φSa3**, the β-haemolysin-converting phage, and
it carries the human immune-evasion cluster:

```{r iec}
meta |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_10820", "B7H15_10840", "B7H15_10845",
                          "B7H15_10875", "B7H15_11175")) |>
  transmute(locus_tag, gene, start_Mb = round(start / 1e6, 3),
            protein = substr(coalesce(up_protein_name, product), 1, 48))
```

The genes that are down in `stp` are the phage's **structural and replication module** —
capsid, portal, tail, terminase, recombinase, DnaD — not the immune-evasion genes at the
left end:

```{r prophage-detail}
ab_mean <- ab |>
  group_by(locus_tag, genotype) |>
  summarise(mu = mean(normalized_abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_obs = sum(!is.na(normalized_abundance)), .groups = "drop")

ab_mean |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = genotype, values_from = c(mu, n_obs)) |>
  inner_join(select(meta, locus_tag, start, product), by = "locus_tag") |>
  filter(start > 2.1e6, start < 2.125e6, n_obs_anc >= 6, n_obs_stp >= 3) |>
  transmute(locus_tag, start_Mb = round(start / 1e6, 3),
            `stp − anc` = round(mu_stp - mu_anc, 2),
            `stk − anc` = round(mu_stk - mu_anc, 2),
            n_anc = n_obs_anc, n_stp = n_obs_stp,
            product = substr(product, 1, 34)) |>
  arrange(start_Mb)
```

```{r prophage-per-sample}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Same per-sample view for the prophage structural module."

ab |>
  mutate(region = case_when(start > 2.103e6 & start < 2.125e6 ~ "prophage",
                            start < 2.08e6 | start > 2.14e6   ~ "rest",
                            TRUE ~ NA_character_)) |>
  filter(!is.na(region)) |>
  group_by(sample, genotype, medium, region) |>
  summarise(md = median(normalized_abundance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = region, values_from = md) |>
  mutate(shift = prophage - rest) |>
  ggplot(aes(medium, shift, colour = genotype)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GENOTYPE_COLOURS) +
  labs(y = "prophage minus rest (log2)", x = NULL,
       title = "phiSa3 structural proteins are low in all 9 stp samples")
```

Again: all nine `stp` samples, all three media, no overlap with the other strains. But note
the important difference to the block — these proteins are **still detected** in `stp`
(`n_stp` is often 8 or 9 of 9), just 2–5× lower. So the phage is **not deleted** from the
`stp` strain; it is **less active**.

The most likely reading: in a growing *S. aureus* culture a small fraction of cells
spontaneously induce their prophage (an SOS-type event) and lyse, and the phage structural
proteins we see are the sum of that. A lower level in `stp` means **less spontaneous φSa3
induction** in that strain. Whether that is a consequence of losing Stp1/Stk1 signalling or
simply a property of this particular NTML isolate, we cannot tell from these data. A
plaque/induction assay (± mitomycin C) would answer it directly.

::: {.callout-note}
## Keep remembering what the `stp` strain is
Notebook 07 showed that `stp` (NE1919) has lost **both** Stp1 and — through a polar effect
on the shared operon — most of Stk1. Every `stp` result in this notebook is a
double-mutant result.
:::

## 4. Part C — the interaction contrasts

Now the part that was the actual motivation. The hypothesis was: *if these regions matter,
they should also show up in `interaction_stp_vs_anc_at_PASN_vs_TSB` and
`interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_PASN_vs_TSB`.*

In our tables those contrasts are named the other way around,
`interaction_*_at_TSB_vs_SN` — same thing with the sign flipped:

```{r int-explain}
cat(explain_contrast("interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN"))
```

Run exactly the same scan:

```{r manhattan-int}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "The same genomic scan on the two interaction contrasts."

manhattan(dea, CONTRASTS_INT)
```

```{r int-scan}
scans |>
  filter(contrast %in% CONTRASTS_INT) |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  summarise(threshold = round(first(threshold), 2),
            `windows above threshold` = sum(is_peak), .groups = "drop")
```

### 4.1 The regions are gone — and that is the informative result

```{r cancellation}
dea |>
  mutate(region = case_when(start > BLOCK[1] & start < BLOCK[2] ~ "stk block",
                            start > 2.103e6 & start < 2.125e6   ~ "phiSa3 module",
                            TRUE ~ "rest of genome")) |>
  filter(contrast %in% c("stk_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stk_vs_anc_at_SNpulse", "stk_vs_anc_at_SN",
                         "stp_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stp_vs_anc_at_SNpulse", "stp_vs_anc_at_SN",
                         CONTRASTS_INT)) |>
  group_by(contrast, region) |>
  summarise(median_diff = round(median(diff), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = region, values_from = median_diff) |>
  select(contrast, `stk block`, `phiSa3 module`, `rest of genome`)
```

Read that table top to bottom. The `stk` block is at +0.72 / +0.66 / +0.72 in the three
media — and at **−0.07 and +0.03** in the two interaction contrasts. It is gone.

The φSa3 module is a more honest, messier case: it is down in `stp` in all three media
(−0.45 / −0.18 / −0.37) but **not equally**, so a residue of about −0.26 survives into the
interaction. That residue is real and it is why a couple of phage proteins still appear in
the interaction hit list. Mostly constitutive, partly not.

This is not a failure of the idea; it is the **arithmetic of an interaction contrast
working as designed**. An interaction is a difference of differences. Anything that is
constant between media — a gene dosage difference, a prophage that is equally quiet in all
media, a strain background effect — cancels exactly:

$$(\text{stk}-\text{anc})_{\text{TSB}} - (\text{stk}-\text{anc})_{\text{SN}} = 0 \quad \text{if the offset is the same in both media}$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## The methodological punchline for the group
Your two peaks are real, reproducible, and they are **strain** differences rather than
**signalling** differences. The interaction contrast is the right tool to tell those apart,
because it is blind to anything constitutive. So the answer to "should these regions also
come out in the interaction?" is **no, and the fact that they don't is the evidence that
they are genomic**. Use the interaction contrasts as the clean read-out of
"what do the mutants *do differently* in PASN".
:::

### 4.2 What *does* come out of the interaction contrasts

```{r int-hits}
int_hits <- dea |>
  filter(contrast %in% CONTRASTS_INT, FDR < FDR_CUTOFF, abs(diff) > LFC_CUTOFF)

int_hits |>
  count(contrast, direction = if_else(diff > 0, "larger gap in TSB", "larger gap in SN"))
```

```{r int-top}
int_hits |>
  filter(estimate_type == "observed") |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  slice_max(abs(diff), n = 12) |>
  transmute(contrast, locus_tag, gene, start_Mb = round(start / 1e6, 2),
            diff = round(diff, 2), FDR = signif(FDR, 2),
            protein = substr(coalesce(up_protein_name, product), 1, 40)) |>
  arrange(contrast, desc(abs(diff)))
```

Ranking by raw magnitude is not very informative here: the most extreme values belong to
proteins with thin coverage, where one group mean rests on one or two measurements. The
pattern only becomes visible when you stop looking at the top 12 and ask what the 157 hit proteins
have in common — which is what STRING does in part D. One thing worth noting already is
that iron- and haem-related proteins keep appearing:

```{r iron-hits}
int_hits |>
  filter(str_detect(coalesce(up_protein_name, product),
                    regex("iron|heme|hemin|siderophore|staphyloferrin", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  transmute(contrast = str_remove(contrast, "^interaction_"), locus_tag, gene,
            diff = round(diff, 2), FDR = signif(FDR, 2),
            protein = substr(up_protein_name, 1, 44)) |>
  arrange(gene)
```

### 4.3 One case study, done properly: the *kdp* operon

`kdp` is the strongest single hit in `interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN`
(`kdpB` diff = +5.3). Before believing a number that large, look at the raw values —
`CLAUDE.md` rule 4.

```{r kdp-raw}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Per-sample normalised abundances for the kdp operon. Each point is one sample."
plot_protein(c("B7H15_11530", "B7H15_11535", "B7H15_11540", "B7H15_11550", "B7H15_11555"), ab)
```

```{r kdp-n}
ab |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_11530", "B7H15_11535", "B7H15_11540",
                          "B7H15_11550", "B7H15_11555")) |>
  group_by(locus_tag, genotype, medium) |>
  summarise(n_detected = sum(!is.na(normalized_abundance)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(genotype, medium), values_from = n_detected) |>
  inner_join(select(meta, locus_tag, gene), by = "locus_tag") |>
  relocate(gene, .after = locus_tag)
```

Read the counts: in **TSB** and **SNpulse** every group has 3 of 3, and there `kdp` is
cleanly up in `stk` by ~2 log2 (4×). In **SN**, detection collapses to 1–3 of 3 in most
groups. The enormous interaction value is therefore mostly driven by the *SN* side, where
it rests on one or two measurements per group.

**So the honest statement is:** `kdp` is solidly elevated in `stk` in TSB and SNpulse;
whether it genuinely inverts in SN is not established by these data. And note the
confounder from part B — `kdp` sits **inside the amplified block**, so part of its baseline
elevation is gene dosage. The block median is +0.7, the `kdp` effect is +2.2, so there is a
real surplus on top of dosage, but the two cannot be separated with proteomics alone.

KdpD/KdpE is a potassium-sensing two-component system that in *S. aureus* also regulates
virulence genes (STRING annotation below). A two-component histidine kinase being
differentially abundant in a Ser/Thr-kinase mutant is a nice link to the course's
phospho-signalling theme — and a nice thing to check in the phospho data set.

## 5. Part D — STRING: the extended network and enrichment

We map our locus tags to STRING via the NCTC 8325 UniProt orthologs that ship in the
metadata table (keeping only `ortholog_quality == "good"`), then use the STRING v12 REST
API. Everything is cached under `data/derived/string_cache/`, so a second render does not
hit the network.

```{r string-helper}
STRING_SPECIES <- 93061   # S. aureus NCTC 8325, the reference STRING genome
CACHE <- file.path(REPO_ROOT, "data", "derived", "string_cache")
dir.create(CACHE, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

string_api <- function(endpoint, params) {
  key <- paste(names(params), unlist(params), collapse = "&")
  f <- file.path(CACHE, paste0(endpoint, "_", substr(openssl::md5(key), 1, 16), ".tsv"))
  if (file.exists(f)) return(read_tsv(f, show_col_types = FALSE))
  res <- httr::POST(paste0("https://string-db.org/api/tsv/", endpoint),
                    body = c(params, list(species = STRING_SPECIES,
                                          caller_identity = "bio253_course")),
                    encode = "form")
  httr::stop_for_status(res)
  x <- read_tsv(I(httr::content(res, "text", encoding = "UTF-8")), show_col_types = FALSE)
  write_tsv(x, f)
  x
}
```

```{r string-map}
# The background for any enrichment test must be "what we could have detected",
# not "the whole genome".
detected <- meta |>
  filter(protein_key %in% dea$protein_key, ortholog_quality == "good", !is.na(uniprot_acc))

mapped <- string_api("get_string_ids",
                     list(identifiers = paste(unique(detected$uniprot_acc), collapse = "\r"),
                          limit = 1, echo_query = 1)) |>
  select(uniprot_acc = queryItem, string_id = stringId, string_name = preferredName) |>
  distinct(uniprot_acc, .keep_all = TRUE)

detected <- inner_join(detected, mapped, by = "uniprot_acc")

tibble(step = c("proteins quantified", "with a good NCTC 8325 ortholog",
                "mapped to a STRING identifier"),
       n = c(n_distinct(dea$protein_key),
             n_distinct(filter(meta, protein_key %in% dea$protein_key,
                               ortholog_quality == "good", !is.na(uniprot_acc))$protein_key),
             nrow(detected)))
```

### 5.1 Enrichment of the interaction hits

```{r string-enrich}
hit_nodes <- int_hits |> distinct(protein_key) |> inner_join(detected, by = "protein_key")

enrich <- string_api("enrichment",
                     list(identifiers = paste(hit_nodes$string_id, collapse = "\r"),
                          background_string_identifiers = paste(detected$string_id, collapse = "\r")))

# PMID terms are text-mining co-citation, not function -- drop them.
enrich_fn <- enrich |> filter(category != "PMID", fdr < 0.05) |> arrange(fdr)

enrich_fn |>
  transmute(category, description = substr(description, 1, 46),
            hits = number_of_genes, background = number_of_genes_in_background,
            FDR = signif(fdr, 2),
            genes = substr(preferredNames, 1, 46))
```

Against a properly chosen background the signature is narrow and very consistent:
**secreted, signal-peptide-bearing, cell-wall-anchored and extracellular proteins**
(21 of the 69 detected "Secreted" proteins are hits), plus **potassium transport**
(`kdpA/B/C`, 3 of 3) and **branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis** (`ilvA/D`, `leuA/B`).

::: {.callout-caution}
## What the background does — and a claim I had to withdraw
With the *whole genome* as background, this hit list also looks strongly "iron-enriched".
With the **detected proteome** as background it does not: no iron or haem GO/KEGG term
reaches FDR < 0.05. The Isd proteins are abundant, easily detected surface proteins, so
they are over-represented in *any* list drawn from this data set. They are genuinely in
the hit list (see §4.2) and they are worth following up — but "iron acquisition is
enriched" is **not** supported once the background is right. This is the single most
common way enrichment analysis misleads, and it is worth showing rather than hiding.
:::

So the defensible answer to "what do the mutants do differently on the proteome level in
PASN" is: **the medium-dependent divergence is concentrated in the secreted and
cell-surface compartment**, not in the cytoplasmic housekeeping machinery. Given that PASN
is partly nutrient-depleted and full of *P. aeruginosa* exoproducts, a different
re-tuning of the envelope and the secretome is a biologically sensible place for the two
signalling mutants to differ from the wild type.

```{r enrich-plot}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "STRING enrichment of the interaction hits against the detected-proteome background (PMID text-mining terms excluded)."

enrich_fn |>
  slice_min(fdr, n = 12) |>
  mutate(description = forcats::fct_reorder(substr(description, 1, 42), -log10(fdr))) |>
  ggplot(aes(-log10(fdr), description, fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(y = NULL, x = "-log10(FDR)", fill = NULL)
```

### 5.2 The extended network

We ask STRING for the high-confidence interactions among our hits, and let it **add 15
proteins of its own** that connect them — that is the "extended" part: proteins we did not
find ourselves but that STRING says belong in the picture.

```{r string-network}
net <- string_api("network", list(identifiers = paste(hit_nodes$string_id, collapse = "\r"),
                                  add_nodes = 15, required_score = 700))

added <- setdiff(unique(c(net$preferredName_A, net$preferredName_B)), hit_nodes$string_name)
tibble(edges = nrow(net),
       nodes = n_distinct(c(net$preferredName_A, net$preferredName_B)),
       `added by STRING` = length(added))
added
```

`kdpE`, `leuC`, `leuD` and `ilvC` are among them — STRING completes the `kdp` two-component
system and the branched-chain amino acid pathway that our hit list only sampled. That is
the extended network earning its keep.

```{r network-plot}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Extended STRING network (confidence >= 0.7) of the interaction hits. Colour = direction in the interaction contrasts; grey = added by STRING. Only components with at least 3 members are drawn."

g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  select(net, preferredName_A, preferredName_B, score), directed = FALSE) |>
  # STRING reports every edge twice (A-B and B-A); keep one, keep the score
  igraph::simplify(edge.attr.comb = list(score = "max"))

# keep components of size >= 3 so the picture stays readable
comp <- igraph::components(g)
g <- igraph::induced_subgraph(g, which(comp$membership %in% which(comp$csize >= 3)))

node_info <- int_hits |>
  inner_join(detected, by = "protein_key") |>
  group_by(string_name) |>
  summarise(diff = diff[which.max(abs(diff))], .groups = "drop")

set.seed(7)
lay <- igraph::layout_with_fr(g)
nodes <- tibble(name = igraph::V(g)$name, x = lay[, 1], y = lay[, 2]) |>
  left_join(node_info, by = c("name" = "string_name"))

edges <- igraph::as_data_frame(g, "edges") |>
  left_join(select(nodes, name, x, y), by = c("from" = "name")) |>
  left_join(select(nodes, name, xend = x, yend = y), by = c("to" = "name"))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, alpha = score),
               colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y, fill = diff), shape = 21, size = 4.2,
             colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = 2.9,
                           max.overlaps = 40, segment.size = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#0072B2", mid = "grey92", high = "#D55E00",
                       midpoint = 0, na.value = "grey80",
                       name = "interaction\nlog2 FC") +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.25, 0.9), guide = "none") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The drawing is worth reading module by module. Four stand out:

* **`kdpA/B/C/D/E`** — the complete potassium system, with `kdpE` supplied by STRING.
* **`isdA`–`isdB`–`isdC`–`srtB`** — the haem-uptake surface module and its sortase.
* a large **amino-acid / central-carbon module** around `ilvA/C/D`, `leuA/B/C/D`, `tdcB`,
  `ldh1`, `pflA/B` — where STRING contributed `ilvC`, `leuC` and `leuD` to complete the
  branched-chain pathway our hit list only sampled.
* **`purC/F/M/S`** (purine biosynthesis) and a small **`argF`–`arcA`** arginine-catabolism
  triangle, neither of which stood out in the enrichment table.

Note what is *not* in the picture: most of the secreted proteins that drove the enrichment
(`hly`, `sbi`, `splF`, `isaA`, the Ssl proteins) are singletons or pairs here and were
dropped by the "components of ≥ 3" filter. Secreted virulence factors are co-regulated
rather than physically interacting, so STRING's high-confidence edges do not connect them.
**Enrichment and network tell you different things**, and here they genuinely disagree
about what the headline is — worth keeping both.

::: {.callout-caution}
## What STRING is and is not
STRING edges are mostly **predictions** — from genomic neighbourhood, co-occurrence,
co-expression and text mining — not measured interactions in *this* experiment. Two
proteins joined here need not touch each other. Use the network to generate hypotheses
and to see modules, never as evidence that something physically binds. Also note we mapped
through NCTC 8325 orthologs, so JE2-specific proteins (the whole φSa3 and SaPI content,
for instance) are under-represented by construction.
:::

### 5.3 Clustering and cluster labels — straight from the API

On the STRING website you can apply a clustering (k-means, MCL or Leiden) and switch on a
*cluster name overlay*. **Both are available through the API**, which is not obvious,
because they do not live on the `network` endpoint — they are parameters of the
**network image** endpoint:

| parameter | what it does |
|---|---|
| `network_clustering_algorithm` | `kmeans`, `MCL` or `leiden` (default: no clustering) |
| `network_clustering_parameter_kmeans` | k-means: number of clusters (default 3) |
| `network_clustering_parameter_mcl` | MCL: inflation; higher = more, smaller clusters (default 3) |
| `network_clustering_parameter_leiden` | Leiden: resolution; higher = more, smaller clusters (default 1) |
| `cluster_aware_layout` | lay the network out so each cluster forms its own group (0/1) |
| `network_clustering_edge_visibility` | edges *between* clusters: `faded`, `dotted`, `solid`, `noshow` |
| `show_cluster_names` | the overlay: names each cluster after its most characteristic functional terms (0/1) |
| `cluster_name_size` | 1, 1.5, 2 … 6 (default grows with the picture width) |

The important part for us is that the clustering is not only available as a *picture*.
The **`network_image_url`** endpoint takes exactly the same parameters and returns, as
TSV/JSON/XML, **one row per cluster**: its number, colour, size, the member proteins and —
crucially — `clusterNames`, the same labels that the overlay draws. So you can have the
clusters as *data*.

```{r string-image-helper}
# The image endpoints return bytes, not a table, so they need their own helper.
# `endpoint` is "image/network" (PNG), "highres_image/network" or "svg/network".
string_file <- function(endpoint, params, file) {
  path <- file.path(CACHE, file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    res <- httr::POST(paste0("https://string-db.org/api/", endpoint),
                      body = c(params, list(species = STRING_SPECIES,
                                            caller_identity = "bio253_course")),
                      encode = "form")
    httr::stop_for_status(res)
    writeBin(httr::content(res, "raw"), path)
  }
  path
}

# One parameter set, used for BOTH the picture and the cluster table, so they match.
cluster_params <- list(
  identifiers                         = paste(hit_nodes$string_id, collapse = "\r"),
  network_flavor                      = "confidence",
  hide_disconnected_nodes             = 1,
  network_clustering_algorithm        = "leiden",
  network_clustering_parameter_leiden = 1.4,
  cluster_aware_layout                = 1,
  network_clustering_edge_visibility  = "faded",
  show_cluster_names                  = 1,
  cluster_name_size                   = 1
)
```

```{r string-clusters}
clusters <- string_api("network_image_url", cluster_params)

clusters |>
  transmute(cluster = clusterNumber, colour = clusterColor, n = proteinCount,
            name = substr(clusterNames, 1, 60),
            members = substr(preferredNames, 1, 52))
```

```{r string-cluster-image}
#| fig-cap: "The same network, clustered with Leiden by STRING itself (resolution 1.4), laid out cluster-aware and labelled with STRING's own cluster names. This is the API reproducing what the website's Clusters panel does."
knitr::include_graphics(string_file("image/network", cluster_params, "leiden_clustered_network.png"))
```

This is the same figure the website produces, and it is a better summary of the hit list
than anything we drew by hand: STRING names the clusters after their most characteristic
functional terms, and the names line up with the enrichment in §5.1 —
**Peptidoglycan-anchor / NEAr transporter domain** (the Isd haem cluster),
**Secreted**, **Potassium transport** (`kdp`), **Valine, leucine and isoleucine
biosynthesis**, **De novo IMP biosynthesis**, **Nitrogen metabolism**,
**Citrulline biosynthesis / arginine metabolism**, **Lipid degradation**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two things worth knowing before you use this
**The clustering depends on the confidence cut-off, sometimes a lot.** The figure above
uses STRING's default score threshold. Re-run it with `required_score = 700` (the
threshold we used in §5.2) and the large secreted/surface clusters fall apart into
singletons, because the edges that hold them together are co-expression and text-mining
links below 0.7 — exactly the point made in §5.2. Neither answer is wrong; they answer
different questions. Report the threshold with the picture.

**TSV drops the image URL.** In `json` format the first record also carries an `imageURL`
field pointing at the rendered PNG (valid for six months); the `tsv` output has the cluster
columns only. If you want the link rather than the bytes, ask for JSON.
:::

Two closing remarks on *which* network figure to use. STRING's clustered image knows the
cluster structure and can name it, but it cannot show **our** measurements. The hand-drawn
network in §5.2 colours every node by its interaction fold change, which is the thing we
actually measured, but it has no cluster labels. They are complementary, and a report is
usually better with both than with either alone.

### 5.4 Putting our fold changes on STRING's own figure, as halos

The clustered figure above is STRING's. It knows the clusters and names them, but it knows
nothing about *our* experiment. The hand-drawn network in §5.2 knows our fold changes but
has no cluster labels. We can have both — because the API also serves the network as
**SVG**, and an SVG is text we can edit.

The trick is that every node in STRING's SVG is a `<g>` element that carries its own
identity and position as data attributes:

```
<g class='nwnodecontainer' data-safe_div_label='kdpB'
   data-x_pos='394' data-y_pos='284' data-radius='20' id='node.14505777'>
```

So we can walk the nodes, look each one up in our DEA table, and inject coloured discs
*behind* each node. And because we can inject more than one disc, we can show **two**
contrasts at once: draw the larger disc first and the smaller one on top of it, and what
is left visible is a pair of concentric rings. Outer ring = the `stk` interaction, inner
ring = the `stp` interaction, node fill = STRING's cluster colour.

That is worth doing here, because the two interaction contrasts are much less redundant
than they look — most hit proteins are a hit in only one of them, which a single ring
per node hides completely:

```{r halo-overlap}
int_hits |>
  mutate(ring = if_else(str_detect(contrast, "stk"), "stk", "stp")) |>
  distinct(protein_key, ring) |>
  count(protein_key, name = "in_n_contrasts") |>
  count(in_n_contrasts, name = "proteins")
```

```{r halo-params}
# Same clustering as above; flat nodes keep the file ~20x smaller than the
# default structure thumbnails, and make the halos easier to read.
halo_params <- c(cluster_params,
                 list(block_structure_pics_in_bubbles = 1, flat_node_design = 1))

svg_text <- readLines(string_file("svg/network", halo_params, "leiden_flat_network.svg"),
                      warn = FALSE) |>
  paste(collapse = "\n")
```

```{r halo-values}
# Two rings means two numbers per node. Note one deliberate difference from the
# node colours in 5.2: nodes were *selected* by significance, but a ring is
# coloured by the measured effect in that contrast whether or not it is
# significant. Otherwise grey would mean two different things ("not measured"
# and "measured, but not a hit"). Significance is shown by the ring outline instead.
int_values <- dea |>
  filter(contrast %in% CONTRASTS_INT) |>
  inner_join(detected, by = "protein_key") |>
  mutate(ring   = if_else(str_detect(contrast, "stk"), "stk", "stp"),
         is_hit = FDR < FDR_CUTOFF & abs(diff) > LFC_CUTOFF) |>
  group_by(string_name, ring) |>
  slice_max(abs(diff), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(string_name, ring, diff, is_hit)
```

```{r halo-build}
LIMIT <- 4                                   # clip the colour scale at +/- 4 log2
ramp <- colorRamp(c("#0072B2", "#F2F2F2", "#D55E00"))
colour_of <- function(v) {
  if (is.na(v)) return("#BFBFBF")            # STRING-added, or not measured here
  t <- (max(min(v, LIMIT), -LIMIT) + LIMIT) / (2 * LIMIT)
  rgb(ramp(t)[1], ramp(t)[2], ramp(t)[3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

# Outer ring first, inner ring second. Each disc paints over the middle of the
# previous one, so two filled circles end up reading as two concentric rings.
RINGS <- c(stk = 10, stp = 5)                # pixels added to the node radius

node_tags <- regmatches(svg_text,
                        gregexpr("<g class='nwnodecontainer'[^>]*>", svg_text))[[1]]
attr_of <- function(tag, a) sub(paste0(".*", a, "='([^']*)'.*"), "\\1", tag)

for (tag in node_tags) {
  label <- attr_of(tag, "data-safe_div_label")
  r0    <- as.numeric(attr_of(tag, "data-radius"))
  discs <- vapply(names(RINGS), function(ring) {
    i   <- match(paste(label, ring), paste(int_values$string_name, int_values$ring))
    hit <- !is.na(i) && int_values$is_hit[i]
    sprintf("<circle cx='%s' cy='%s' r='%.1f' fill='%s' stroke='%s' stroke-width='%.1f' />",
            attr_of(tag, "data-x_pos"), attr_of(tag, "data-y_pos"), r0 + RINGS[[ring]],
            colour_of(if (is.na(i)) NA_real_ else int_values$diff[i]),
            if (hit) "rgb(30,30,30)" else "rgb(160,160,160)",
            if (hit) 1.6 else 0.6)
  }, character(1))
  # inserted right after the opening tag, so both are painted BEHIND the node
  svg_text <- sub(tag, paste0(tag, "\n", paste(discs, collapse = "\n")),
                  svg_text, fixed = TRUE)
}
```

```{r halo-coverage}
labels_in_figure <- vapply(node_tags, attr_of, character(1), "data-safe_div_label")
key <- paste(int_values$string_name, int_values$ring)

tibble(ring        = c("outer: stk interaction", "inner: stp interaction"),
       nodes_in_figure = length(node_tags),
       measured    = c(sum(paste(labels_in_figure, "stk") %in% key),
                       sum(paste(labels_in_figure, "stp") %in% key)),
       a_hit       = c(sum(paste(labels_in_figure, "stk") %in% key[int_values$is_hit]),
                       sum(paste(labels_in_figure, "stp") %in% key[int_values$is_hit])))
```

```{r halo-legend}
# STRING's SVG has width/height but no viewBox. Read them, then add a strip at
# the bottom for the legend and give the file a viewBox so it scales cleanly.
wh <- as.numeric(c(sub(".*\\bwidth='([0-9]+)'.*",  "\\1", substr(svg_text, 1, 400)),
                   sub(".*\\bheight='([0-9]+)'.*", "\\1", substr(svg_text, 1, 400))))
LEGEND_H <- 160

legend_svg <- paste0(
  # the colour bar
  paste(vapply(0:59, function(i) {
    v <- -LIMIT + 2 * LIMIT * i / 59
    sprintf("<rect x='%.1f' y='34' width='3.3' height='14' fill='%s' />",
            20 + i * 3.2, colour_of(v))
  }, character(1)), collapse = ""),
  "<rect x='20' y='34' width='192' height='14' fill='none' stroke='rgb(80,80,80)' stroke-width='0.7'/>",
  "<text x='116' y='26' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>interaction log2 fold change</text>",
  sprintf("<text x='20'  y='64' font-size='13'>-%d</text>", LIMIT),
  sprintf("<text x='212' y='64' font-size='13' text-anchor='end'>+%d</text>", LIMIT),
  # a schematic node: outer ring, inner ring, node fill
  "<circle cx='300' cy='60' r='30' fill='#D55E00' stroke='rgb(30,30,30)' stroke-width='1.6'/>",
  "<circle cx='300' cy='60' r='20' fill='#0072B2' stroke='rgb(30,30,30)' stroke-width='1.6'/>",
  "<circle cx='300' cy='60' r='11' fill='#9fcf9f' stroke='rgb(70,70,70)' stroke-width='0.8'/>",
  "<text x='346' y='36' font-size='13'>outer ring = interaction_stk_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN</text>",
  "<text x='346' y='58' font-size='13'>inner ring = interaction_stp_vs_anc_at_TSB_vs_SN</text>",
  "<text x='346' y='80' font-size='13'>node fill   = STRING cluster colour</text>",
  # what the ring outline means
  "<text x='346' y='104' font-size='13'>thick dark outline = FDR &lt; 0.1 and |log2FC| &gt; 1 in that contrast</text>",
  "<text x='346' y='126' font-size='13'>thin pale outline  = measured, but not a hit in that contrast</text>")

svg_text <- sub("</svg>\\s*$",
                sprintf("<g id='halo-legend' transform='translate(0,%d)'>%s</g></svg>",
                        wh[2], legend_svg),
                svg_text)
svg_text <- sub("height='[0-9]+'", sprintf("height='%d'", wh[2] + LEGEND_H), svg_text)
svg_text <- sub("<svg ", sprintf("<svg viewBox='0 0 %d %d' ", wh[1], wh[2] + LEGEND_H),
                svg_text)
```

```{r halo-show}
#| fig-cap: "STRING's Leiden clusters and cluster names, with both interaction contrasts added as halos. Node fill = cluster colour; outer ring = stk interaction; inner ring = stp interaction; thick dark outline = a hit in that contrast."
# Write the edited SVG and let Quarto embed it. (Pasting the SVG inline into the
# HTML also works, but pandoc lower-cases `viewBox`, which SVG then ignores.)
halo_svg <- file.path(CACHE, "leiden_flat_network_halos.svg")
writeLines(svg_text, halo_svg)
knitr::include_graphics(halo_svg)
```

Read each node from the inside out: STRING's cluster colour, then the `stp` interaction,
then the `stk` interaction. Three patterns are now visible that one ring could not show.

* **The potassium cluster is almost purely a `stk` effect.** `kdpB` and `kdpD` have an
  outer ring at the top of the scale (+5.3 and +5.1, FDR 0.083 and 2.2e-07) and an inner
  ring that is essentially white (+0.07 and +0.60, both far from significant). Only `kdpC`
  is a hit in both. Whatever the `kdp` system is doing, it tracks the loss of the kinase,
  not the loss of the phosphatase.
* **Branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis leans the same way, but not exclusively.**
  `ilvA` is strongly up in both (+3.01 and +2.32, both FDR < 0.002); `leuA`, `leuB` and
  `ilvD` are `stk`-only. So the cluster is orange on the outside and mixed on the inside.
* **The haem genes split, and in opposite directions.** `hrtA` is one of the strongest
  `stp` results in the whole table (-4.98, FDR 0.014) while its `stk` ring is blank
  (+0.70, FDR 0.84); its operon partner `hrtB` does the reverse (+2.83, FDR 0.076 in
  `stk`; +0.36, FDR 0.86 in `stp`). Two subunits of one transporter pointing opposite ways
  in two contrasts is a warning sign, not a finding — check `plot_protein()` for both
  before building any story on it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A correction to what I wrote under the one-ring version
With a single ring per node I took, for each protein, the interaction contrast with the
larger |log2FC| — and then described `hrtA` and `hrtB` as "ringed in deep blue". That was
wrong: only `hrtA` was blue, `hrtB` was orange, because they came from *different*
contrasts. That is exactly the failure mode the second ring removes. A one-number-per-node
summary over two contrasts is convenient and quietly mixes sources; if you reduce two
contrasts to one colour, say in the caption which contrast each node came from, or do not
reduce them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this is worth the twenty lines of string manipulation
Any overlay you can compute — fold change, FDR, phospho-site count, presence/absence,
how often a protein shows up across contrasts — can be painted onto STRING's own layout
this way, because the SVG keeps the node identity and coordinates in the markup. You get
STRING's clustering and labels *and* your data in one figure, without reimplementing
either. `RINGS` is the whole control: drop an entry for a single ring, add one (with a
larger offset, listed first) for a third contrast. Past three the rings get thin — at that
point use a small pie or a bar glyph per node instead, which is the same injection trick
with a different shape.
:::

## 6. Part E — does the phospho layer agree?

The total proteome says *how much* protein there is. The phospho-enriched samples say
something the total proteome cannot: whether a protein is **modified**. Three questions:

1. Does the phospho data independently confirm the `stk` amplification? (**yes**)
2. Do the interaction hits carry phospho-sites that move? (**no — coverage is too thin**)
3. Does the phospho layer have an interaction signal of its own? (**yes, a different one**)

### 6.0 First, an honest coverage check

```{r phospho-coverage}
sites <- read_sites("STYH")

site_detection <- sites |>
  group_by(site_id, protein_key, locus_tag, residue, position) |>
  summarise(n_det = sum(!is.na(intensity)), .groups = "drop")

tibble(
  what = c("sites in the table", "proteins carrying them",
           "sites detected in >= 9 of 27 samples", "sites detected in >= 18 of 27",
           "sites seen in exactly ONE sample",
           "rows of the phospho DEA that are LOD-imputed (%)"),
  n = c(n_distinct(site_detection$site_id),
        n_distinct(site_detection$protein_key),
        sum(site_detection$n_det >= 9),
        sum(site_detection$n_det >= 18),
        sum(site_detection$n_det == 1),
        round(100 * mean(read_dea("phospho_STYH")$estimate_type == "lod_imputed")))
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Read this before any phospho conclusion
Of 4,245 sites, **only 565 are detected in at least a third of the samples**, and 1,865 are
one-hit wonders. **96 % of the phospho DEA rows are LOD-imputed**, i.e. presence/absence
rather than a measured fold change. Everything below is therefore restricted to the 565
well-detected sites, and imputed estimates are always flagged. With n = 3 and this much
missingness, the phospho layer can *support* a hypothesis and can give strong
presence/absence evidence — it cannot deliver precise fold changes.
:::

### 6.1 The amplified block, seen a second time

The phospho samples were enriched and measured separately, so they are an independent
look. Site intensities come straight from FragPipe and are *not* cross-run normalised, so
we median-centre each sample first, then compare each site's mean in `stk` against `anc`.

```{r phospho-block}
site_norm <- sites |>
  group_by(sample) |>
  # FragPipe intensities are not normalised across runs; centre each run first.
  mutate(norm = log2_intensity - median(log2_intensity, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  inner_join(select(meta, protein_key, start), by = "protein_key")

site_geno <- site_norm |>
  filter(!is.na(norm)) |>
  group_by(site_id, protein_key, start, genotype) |>
  summarise(mu = mean(norm), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 2) |>                      # at least 2 of 3 replicates in that genotype
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = genotype, values_from = mu) |>
  filter(!is.na(anc), !is.na(stk)) |>
  mutate(stk_minus_anc = stk - anc,
         region = if_else(start > BLOCK[1] & start < BLOCK[2], "block", "rest"))

site_geno |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(sites = n(),
            `median stk - anc` = round(median(stk_minus_anc), 2),
            `fold change` = round(2^median(stk_minus_anc), 2), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r phospho-block-test}
wilcox.test(stk_minus_anc ~ region, data = site_geno)
```

```{r phospho-block-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Per-site stk-vs-anc difference, sites inside the amplified block vs the rest. Independent measurement, same conclusion."

ggplot(site_geno, aes(stk_minus_anc, region, fill = region)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.size = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(block = "#D55E00", rest = "grey80"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "phospho-site log2 difference, stk minus anc", y = NULL)
```

The 50 well-covered sites inside the block sit **+0.45 log2 (1.36x)** above the `anc`
samples, against **+0.04** for the 728 sites elsewhere. This is a different sample
preparation, a different enrichment chemistry and a different normalisation, and it
reproduces the block. Combined with the sharp *rrn* boundaries and the presence in all 9
`stk` samples, the amplification hypothesis is now considerably better supported.

(The shift is smaller than the +0.72 seen on proteins. Do not over-read that — site
intensity is protein abundance × occupancy, the dynamic range of the enriched samples is
different, and 50 sites is not many. The direction and the contrast with the rest of the
genome are the result; the exact number is not.)

### 6.2 The interaction hits: coverage is simply not there

Now the question that motivated this section — do the 157 interaction-hit proteins carry
sites that move in the same comparisons?

```{r phospho-hits}
hit_proteins <- int_hits |> distinct(protein_key)

tibble(
  what = c("interaction hit proteins (total proteome)",
           "of those, with ANY phospho-site in the table",
           "of those, with a site detected in >= 9 of 27 samples"),
  n = c(nrow(hit_proteins),
        n_distinct(site_detection$protein_key[site_detection$protein_key %in% hit_proteins$protein_key]),
        n_distinct(site_detection$protein_key[site_detection$protein_key %in% hit_proteins$protein_key &
                                              site_detection$n_det >= 9]))
)
```

Fifteen proteins out of 157. And for those fifteen, the site-level interaction estimates
are almost all non-significant or imputed:

```{r phospho-hits-detail}
well_covered <- site_detection |> filter(n_det >= 9)

site_vs_protein <- read_dea("phospho_STYH", contrasts = CONTRASTS_INT) |>
  filter(site_id %in% well_covered$site_id) |>
  select(site_id, protein_key, contrast, site_diff = diff,
         site_FDR = FDR, site_type = estimate_type) |>
  inner_join(select(int_hits, protein_key, contrast, prot_diff = diff),
             by = c("protein_key", "contrast")) |>
  inner_join(select(meta, protein_key, gene, up_protein_name), by = "protein_key")

site_vs_protein |>
  transmute(contrast = str_remove(contrast, "^interaction_"),
            gene, site = str_extract(site_id, "[STYH]\\d+$"),
            site_diff = round(site_diff, 2), site_FDR = signif(site_FDR, 2), site_type,
            prot_diff = round(prot_diff, 2),
            protein = substr(up_protein_name, 1, 30)) |>
  arrange(site_FDR) |>
  head(10)
```

**So the answer to the original question is no.** The secreted / cell-surface signature
from §5.1 cannot be followed into the phospho data, because secreted and wall-anchored
proteins are poorly represented among the detected phospho-sites in the first place. This
is a limitation of the data, not evidence that those proteins are unphosphorylated.

### 6.3 The phospho layer has its own, different interaction signal

Asking the phospho data directly — without going through the total-proteome hit list —
does give results:

```{r phospho-own}
phospho_int <- read_dea("phospho_STYH", contrasts = CONTRASTS_INT) |>
  filter(site_id %in% well_covered$site_id)

phospho_int |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  summarise(`well-covered sites tested` = n(),
            `observed (not imputed)` = sum(estimate_type == "observed"),
            `FDR < 0.1 and |diff| > 1` = sum(FDR < FDR_CUTOFF & abs(diff) > LFC_CUTOFF),
            .groups = "drop")
```

```{r phospho-own-list}
phospho_sig <- phospho_int |>
  filter(FDR < FDR_CUTOFF, abs(diff) > LFC_CUTOFF) |>
  left_join(select(well_covered, site_id, n_det), by = "site_id") |>
  left_join(select(meta, protein_key, gene, up_protein_name), by = "protein_key") |>
  left_join(select(int_hits, protein_key, contrast, prot_diff = diff),
            by = c("protein_key", "contrast"))

phospho_sig |>
  transmute(contrast = str_remove(contrast, "^interaction_"), gene,
            site = str_extract(site_id, "[STYH]\\d+$"), n_det,
            diff = round(diff, 2), estimate_type, FDR = signif(FDR, 2),
            protein = substr(up_protein_name, 1, 34)) |>
  arrange(contrast, desc(abs(diff)))
```

Two things stand out.

**First, these are mostly central carbon and energy metabolism enzymes** — pyruvate kinase
(`pyk`), enolase (`eno`), glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (`pgi`), the glucose PTS
transporter (`ptsG`), carbamoyl-phosphate synthase (`carB`), dihydroorotase (`pyrC`),
urease (`ureC`), ribosomal protein `rplR`. For almost all of them the **protein level is
flat** in the same contrast, so if these changes are real they are genuine changes in
phosphorylation, not in abundance. That is exactly the kind of result the phospho layer
exists to provide.

**Second, almost none of them overlap the total-proteome hits:**

```{r phospho-overlap}
tibble(
  what = c("proteins with a significant interaction SITE",
           "of those, also total-proteome interaction hits"),
  n = c(n_distinct(phospho_sig$protein_key),
        sum(unique(phospho_sig$protein_key) %in% hit_proteins$protein_key))
)
```

The protein-level and site-level interaction signals are **largely orthogonal**. That is
not a contradiction — changing how much of an enzyme you make and changing whether it is
phosphorylated are different regulatory moves.

::: {.callout-important}
## The large caveat on §6.3
Look at the `estimate_type` column: nearly every one of these is `lod_imputed`. These are
**presence/absence** calls — the site was found in one genotype×medium combination and not
in another — which is why the fold changes are so extreme (+4 to +10 log2). With n = 3,
presence/absence can arise from a single missed identification. Treat this table as a
**candidate list to verify**, not as a result. Verifying it means targeted PRM/MRM on those
specific peptides.
:::

### 6.4 The one result that needs no caveat: ReoM Thr7

While looking through the significant sites, one protein stands out — and it is the best
single result in this whole notebook.

```{r reom}
sites |>
  filter(locus_tag == "B7H15_08845") |>
  group_by(site = str_extract(site_id, "[STYH]\\d+$"), genotype, medium) |>
  summarise(n_detected = sum(!is.na(intensity)),
            mean_log2 = round(mean(log2_intensity, na.rm = TRUE), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(value = if_else(n_detected == 0, "not detected",
                         paste0(mean_log2, " (", n_detected, "/3)"))) |>
  select(-n_detected, -mean_log2) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(genotype, medium), values_from = value)
```

```{r reom-protein}
# Is the PROTEIN also missing in stk? (If it were, this would be trivial.)
read_abundances("total") |>
  filter(locus_tag == "B7H15_08845") |>
  group_by(genotype) |>
  summarise(n_detected = sum(!is.na(normalized_abundance)),
            mean_log2 = round(mean(normalized_abundance, na.rm = TRUE), 2), .groups = "drop")
```

`B7H15_08845` is **ReoM** (NCTC 8325 ortholog Q2FXW0, `reoM`, "peptidoglycan synthesis
regulatory protein"). The phospho-site at **Thr7** is detected in **3 of 3 samples of every
single `anc` and `stp` group**, in all three media — and in **0 of 9 `stk` samples**. The
ReoM *protein* is present at the same level in all three strains (15.8 / 15.9 / 15.1). So
this is not a missing protein; it is a **missing modification**.

```{r reom-plot}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "ReoM Thr7 phospho-site intensity per sample. Absent from every stk sample; unaffected in stp."

sites |>
  filter(locus_tag == "B7H15_08845", str_detect(site_id, "_T7$")) |>
  ggplot(aes(medium, log2_intensity, colour = genotype)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GENOTYPE_COLOURS) +
  labs(y = "log2 intensity of pThr7", x = NULL,
       caption = "stk has no point in any medium: the site is not detected there")
```

Why this matters:

* **ReoM Thr7 is the conserved PASTA-kinase site.** In *Listeria monocytogenes* PrkA
  phosphorylates ReoM at Thr7, and phospho-ReoM protects MurA — the first enzyme of
  peptidoglycan synthesis — from ClpCP-dependent degradation
  ([Wamp et al. 2020, eLife 9:e56048](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.56048)). The same
  Stk–ReoM–MurA axis has been described in *S. aureus*
  ([Hammond et al. 2025, PMC13692261](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13692261)).
* **This is a positive control that the whole experiment worked.** The kinase mutant has
  lost phosphorylation of a known PASTA-kinase substrate, completely and reproducibly, at
  a site localised with probability 1.0. If you doubted whether the Fe-IMAC enrichment and
  the STYH search were giving real biology, this settles it.
* **It says something new about the `stp` strain.** Notebook 07 showed `stp` has lost most
  of its Stk1 protein through the polar effect — here that is a 16-fold reduction
  (12.5 vs 16.6 log2). And yet **ReoM Thr7 is fully phosphorylated in `stp`**, in every
  medium. Residual Stk1, with no Stp1 left to remove the mark, is evidently enough to
  saturate this site. The kinase/phosphatase *balance*, not the kinase amount, sets the
  outcome — which is the central idea of the course topic, visible in one row of data.

```{r reom-caveats}
# T7 and Y12 sit on the SAME tryptic peptide -- they are not independent observations.
sites |>
  filter(locus_tag == "B7H15_08845") |>
  distinct(site_id, residue, position, peptide, best_loc_prob) |>
  mutate(peptide = substr(peptide, 1, 44))
```

Two honest caveats. The neighbouring **Tyr12** site behaves identically, but it sits on the
*same tryptic peptide*, so T7 and Y12 are one observation, not two. And in the
**interaction** contrast ReoM T7 is not significant at all (FDR = 1.0) — because the loss
is constitutive, identical in all three media. Exactly like the genomic blocks in §4.1, the
clearest signalling result in the data set is invisible to an interaction contrast. That is
the same lesson for the third time, and it is worth internalising.

### 6.5 The obvious follow-up prediction, and why it fails here

If ReoM is unphosphorylated in `stk`, ClpCP should degrade MurA, so **MurA should be lower
in `stk`**. Test it:

```{r mura}
dea |>
  filter(contrast %in% c("stk_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stp_vs_anc_at_TSB"),
         locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_11665", "B7H15_11795")) |>
  transmute(contrast, locus_tag, gene, start_Mb = round(start / 1e6, 3),
            diff = round(diff, 2), FDR = signif(FDR, 2)) |>
  arrange(contrast)
```

MurA is **up** in `stk`, by +0.89 and +0.61 — which is simply the block median (+0.72).
And there is the problem: **both MurA/MurZ paralogues sit inside the amplified block**. Gene
dosage pushes MurA up, the ReoM model pushes it down, and with one measurement we cannot
separate the two. So this prediction is not testable in this data set — another reason the
genome sequencing in the next steps is not optional.

## 7. Where this leaves the group

**What held up.** The genomic-position idea is good and the two peaks are real and
reproducible — far more reproducible than a typical single-protein hit, because they rest
on dozens of neighbouring proteins at once.

**What changed.** The two peaks are most likely not about Stk1/Stp1 signalling at all:

| region | what it is | evidence | medium-dependent? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.183–2.291 Mb, up in `stk` | ~107 kb tandem amplification between two *rRNA* operons; contains *sigB*, *atp*, *kdp* | uniform 1.65× over 94 proteins, sharp *rrn* boundaries, all 9 `stk` samples | no — cancels in the interaction |
| 2.103–2.125 Mb, down in `stp` | φSa3 prophage structural module (phage is inserted in *hlb*) | still detected but 2–5× lower, all 9 `stp` samples | mostly not |

So the group's question — "how can these regulated proteins be connected to the transposon
mutants?" — has a provocative answer: **possibly not through the transposon at all**, but
through what else is different about these two NTML isolates.

**What the phospho layer added.** The phospho samples confirm the `stk` block
independently (§6.1), which is the strongest evidence we have that it is genomic. They
*cannot* follow the secreted/surface signature — only 15 of the 157 hit proteins have a
well-covered site (§6.2). But they carry an interaction signal of their own, on central
carbon metabolism enzymes whose protein levels are flat (§6.3), and they deliver one
unambiguous result: **ReoM Thr7 is phosphorylated in every `anc` and `stp` sample and in no
`stk` sample**, with ReoM protein equally abundant in all three strains (§6.4). That is a
known PASTA-kinase substrate behaving exactly as it should, which validates the experiment
— and it shows the `stp` strain keeps this site fully phosphorylated despite having 16-fold
less Stk1, i.e. the kinase/phosphatase *balance* is what matters.

**What is genuinely new from the interaction contrasts.** Once the constitutive strain
differences are removed, what remains is a **secretome / cell-surface**
signature: the mutants and the wild type re-tune their envelope and secreted proteins
differently when they meet PASN. Several iron- and haem-acquisition proteins sit in that
list (`isdA/B/C`, `sbnA/H`, `hrtB`), but note §5.1 — iron is *not* a statistically
enriched category once the detected proteome is used as the background.

### Concrete next steps

1. **Sequence the three strains.** One cheap Illumina run tests the amplification directly
   and checks for other secondary mutations. This is the single highest-value experiment
   this analysis suggests.
2. **Check σ^B^ activity**, since *sigB* sits inside the block: are known σ^B^-regulon
   proteins (e.g. *asp23*, pigment) shifted in `stk` across all media?
3. **Test φSa3 induction** in `stp` directly (± mitomycin C, plaque or qPCR on phage DNA).
4. **Verify the §6.3 candidate sites by targeted MS** (PRM/MRM on the `pyk`, `eno`,
   `pgi`, `ptsG` peptides). They are presence/absence calls today; targeted runs would turn
   them into real measurements, and they are the only interaction-specific *signalling*
   leads we have.
5. **Follow up ReoM properly.** The Stk1-dependence of Thr7 is established here beyond
   reasonable doubt (§6.4). The interesting open question is why `stp` — with 16-fold less
   Stk1 — keeps the site fully phosphorylated. A phosphatase-dead `stp` complement, or
   simply blotting phospho-ReoM across the three strains, would answer it.
6. **Re-plot the scan per medium** (`*_at_SN`, `*_at_SNpulse`) as a control — the block
   must be there in all three, and it is; that is already in §3.1.

A first look at step 2, since it costs two lines. Asp23 (alkaline shock protein 23) is the
classic σ^B^ reporter in *S. aureus*, and conveniently it sits at 2.320 Mb — **outside**
the amplified block, so its own gene dosage is normal:

```{r asp23}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Asp23 and its membrane anchor AmaP, the classic sigma-B reporters, per sample."
plot_protein(c("B7H15_12150", "B7H15_12160"), ab)
```

```{r asp23-diffs}
dea |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% c("B7H15_12150", "B7H15_12160"),
         contrast %in% c("stk_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stk_vs_anc_at_SNpulse", "stk_vs_anc_at_SN",
                         "stp_vs_anc_at_TSB", "stp_vs_anc_at_SNpulse", "stp_vs_anc_at_SN")) |>
  transmute(locus_tag, gene, contrast, diff = round(diff, 2), FDR = signif(FDR, 2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = contrast, values_from = c(diff, FDR)) |>
  select(locus_tag, gene, starts_with("diff"))
```

Two separate results here:

* In **`stk`**, Asp23 is flat (|log2 FC| ≤ 0.18 in all three media) and so is AmaP. So
  there is **no evidence of a globally raised σ^B^ output**, despite the extra *sigB* copy.
  That is a useful negative: an extra gene copy is not the same as more active sigma
  factor — σ^B^ is controlled post-translationally by the RsbU/RsbV/RsbW partner switch,
  and those genes are duplicated along with it, so the stoichiometry may simply be
  preserved.
* In **`stp`**, both Asp23 and AmaP are **down by 0.4–0.6 log2 in every medium**, with very
  small FDRs. The effect is modest but it is the most consistent σ^B^-reporter signal in
  the data, and it is in the strain that lacks both Stp1 and most of Stk1. Worth a proper
  look with more σ^B^ regulon members — a small, genuinely signalling-flavoured lead that
  the two big genomic blocks were drowning out.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
